title: Urbain Grandier Burned at Loudun: Possession Case with Political Dimension
description: Urbain Grandier, priest of Saint-Pierre-du-Marché in Loudun, was burned alive on August 18, 1634 after being convicted of causing the demonic possession of Ursuline nuns at the convent of Loudun. Grandier was a well-connected, educated clergyman who had made enemies through sexual scandals and political maneuvering; the possession case gave his enemies, including Cardinal Richelieu (whom Grandier had allegedly satirized), the means to destroy him. The public exorcisms of possessed nuns attracted thousands of spectators, making this one of the most theatrical cases in witch-trial history. Grandier maintained his innocence through torture and to the stake. Aldous Huxley's The Devils of Loudun (1952) brought the case to broad twentieth-century attention.
historiographical_note: Michel de Certeau's The Possession at Loudun (1970; English 2000) provides the most sophisticated historical analysis, reading the Loudun case as a site of conflict between different systems of authority — clerical, medical, judicial, and state. The case exemplifies the broader pattern identified by historians of possession as a performance: the nuns' possessed behavior was staged in public, shaped by audience expectations, and used by multiple parties for competing ends.
source_method: Contemporary trial records and pamphlets; de Certeau, The Possession at Loudun (1970); secondary scholarship
